The Pacific lamprey Entosphenus tridentatus begins its life cycle with an egg that measures 1.249 millimeters in length and 1.145 millimeters in width, giving rise to a newly hatched larva with an estimated wet weight at birth of just 0.00086 grams [Wwb = 0.00086 grams]. The embryonic development leading to this hatchling proceeds rapidly under warm conditions; when incubated at a constant 18 °C [T = 18 °C], the age at birth is approximately 11 days [ab = approximately 11 days]. This brief embryonic period reflects the accelerated developmental rates characteristic of many anadromous lampreys in relatively elevated thermal regimes. Upon emerging from the egg, the prolarva carries a substantial yolk sac that sustains it through the first days of exogenous feeding. The transition to a free-living ammocoete larva marks the onset of the burrowing, filter-feeding stage that will dominate the species' early life history. Field observations suggest that the initial body mass is remarkably low, even when compared to other agnathan larvae, and that survival through this critical bottleneck may depend heavily on the availability of fine organic detritus and microbial biofilms in depositional stream habitats.

At the onset of gonadal activation, juvenile Pacific lampreys that have completed the protracted ammocoete phase undergo metamorphosis and begin the transition toward reproductive maturity. Data from captive rearing studies indicate that the wet weight at puberty is 3.58 grams [Wwp = 3.58 grams], a modest body mass that is achieved only after several years of larval growth. The total length at puberty, recorded during the early stages of sexual differentiation, has been measured at 14.4 centimeters [Lp = 14.4 centimeters], providing a useful morphometric benchmark for identifying individuals that have initiated the maturation process. This pubertal length is notably smaller than the dimensions of fully grown adults and reflects the species' strategy of reaching reproductive competence at a relatively moderate size before undertaking the oceanic feeding migration. In specimens reared under controlled laboratory conditions at 11 °C [T = 11 °C], the time since birth at puberty has been estimated at roughly 1095 days [tp = roughly 1095 days], a duration that underscores the extended larval period typical of this species. The prolonged interval between hatching and the initiation of metamorphosis appears to be linked to the accumulation of sufficient lipid reserves necessary to fuel the subsequent non-feeding reproductive migration.

Reproductive effort in the Pacific lamprey is characterized by a single, semelparous spawning event at the conclusion of the adult phase. Gravid females produce an extraordinarily large complement of eggs, with ovarian fecundity reaching 238,400 eggs  at the end of life at a temperature of 11 °C [T = 11 °C]. This remarkable egg count is among the highest reported for any anadromous fish species and represents a substantial investment of maternal resources. The production of such a vast number of offspring is presumably an adaptation to high early-life mortality, given the tiny size of the prolarvae at emergence. The fecundity estimate was derived from females that completed their final maturation under thermal conditions approximating 11 °C [T = 11 °C], a temperature that reflects the typical summer stream baseflow in many natal habitats of this species. After spawning, the adults rapidly senesce and die, having expended all their somatic reserves in the construction and deposition of the eggs. This life-history strategy, in which a single, massive reproductive bout is followed by obligate mortality, places extreme selective pressure on the timing and success of the upstream spawning migration.

The ultimate body dimensions attained by Pacific lampreys during their ocean-feeding phase are substantial, reflecting the rich trophic resources available in the marine environment. Maximum recorded total length in adults reaches 76 centimeters [Li = 76 centimeters], a size that is typical for the genus Entosphenus. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight corresponding to this asymptotic length is estimated at 526 grams [Wwi = 526 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions of mature individuals captured during their upstream spawning runs. This represents a nearly 147,000-fold increase in wet mass from the hatchling stage to the fully grown adult, a growth trajectory that underscores the species' capacity for rapid somatic expansion during the marine feeding phase. The length-weight relationship suggests a robust body form relative to some other lamprey species, likely reflecting the muscular build necessary for sustained swimming against swift currents during the spawning migration. Field studies indicate that individuals achieving the maximum length are often the oldest and have presumably spent more than one year at sea. This ultimate size is attained only after the animals have ceased all feeding during the final upstream journey, making stored energy reserves critical for both migration and gamete production.

Longevity records for the Pacific lamprey indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 3285 days [am = approximately 3285 days], or roughly nine years, under natural stream temperature regimes averaging 11 °C [T = 11 °C]. This extended lifespan encompasses the multi-year ammocoete larval phase in freshwater, the metamorphic transformation, the oceanic feeding migration, and the final upstream spawning run. The total duration is notably longer than that of many other anadromous lamprey species, suggesting a slower overall pace of life that may be linked to the relatively cool, productive river systems of the Pacific Northwest. Individuals spend the majority of this nine-year period as burrowing larvae, during which they remain relatively inconspicuous and feed on fine particulate organic matter. The oceanic phase is comparatively brief but critically important for attaining the large body size necessary for high fecundity. After completing the spawning run, the animals die, having fulfilled their single reproductive obligation. This obligate semelparity, combined with the nine-year maximum longevity, positions the Pacific lamprey as an extreme example of a capital-breeding life-history strategy among fishes, where all reproductive energy is acquired before the terminal migration.
